clinicalPearls: Presents in prepubertal children as symmetrical, shiny, glazed erythema with fissuring over the weight-bearing forefoot and plantar surfaces of the great toes.
The instep and the interdigital web spaces are characteristically spared, a pattern that helps distinguish it from tinea pedis and allergic contact dermatitis.
Occlusive synthetic footwear and socks with alternating sweating and rapid drying are central to the process, hence the descriptive term sweaty sock dermatitis.
It is often painful rather than itchy, with a smooth glazed cracked-porcelain appearance and painful fissures that impair walking.
There is an association with atopy, and many affected children have a personal or family history of eczema, asthma or hay fever.
Management centres on reducing occlusion and friction with breathable leather or open footwear, cotton socks, emollients and greasy barrier ointments.
Potassium hydroxide microscopy and fungal culture should be negative and are useful to exclude tinea, which typically involves the web spaces and instep.
The condition tends to settle around puberty, so reassurance about eventual spontaneous resolution is an important part of counselling.
reference.pathophysiology: Juvenile plantar dermatosis is a friction and moisture-related dermatitis of the weight-bearing plantar skin, thought to arise from repeated cycles of hyperhydration and rapid dehydration within occlusive modern footwear and synthetic socks. Sweat is trapped against the skin during activity, then evaporates quickly, and this alternating wetting and drying, combined with mechanical friction on pressure-bearing surfaces, disrupts the stratum corneum barrier of the forefoot. The resulting impaired barrier produces the glazed, fissured appearance. An atopic tendency predisposes to the disorder through an inherently compromised epidermal barrier, and the condition is not primarily allergic or infective, although secondary irritant and, occasionally, contact factors may aggravate it.
additionalDifferentials: tinea pedis with web-space and instep involvement
allergic contact dermatitis to footwear components such as rubber or chromate
additionalInvestigations: potassium hydroxide microscopy and fungal culture of scale to exclude tinea pedis
patch testing when footwear allergic contact dermatitis is suspected
bacterial swab if secondary infection or pitted keratolysis is considered
clinical assessment for atopic stigmata elsewhere on the skin
skin biopsy only in atypical or treatment-resistant cases
examination of footwear and sock materials as part of history
review for koebnerising psoriasis at other sites such as nails and scalp
redFlags: web-space maceration or unilateral disease suggesting tinea rather than juvenile plantar dermatosis
spreading vesiculation or oozing indicating secondary bacterial infection
nail pitting, onycholysis or plaques elsewhere pointing to psoriasis
onset outside the typical prepubertal age range prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
severe painful fissuring limiting mobility and quality of life
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and self-limiting, characteristically improving and resolving spontaneously around puberty. Symptoms fluctuate with footwear and activity, and consistent barrier and footwear measures usually control discomfort in the interim.
pitfalls: misdiagnosing it as tinea pedis and prescribing prolonged antifungals that do not help
overlooking the diagnostic sparing of the instep and web spaces
relying on potent topical corticosteroids alone rather than addressing footwear occlusion and friction
failing to reassure families that resolution around puberty is expected
missing coexisting atopic dermatitis or early psoriasis
